fields.question: Why build CritBank from weak-model errors?
fields.answer: Cluster recurring failures offline into reusable reminders for stronger models. This moves reflection cost upstream and avoids requiring a first failure on each deployed request.
fields.example: Add a common missed-unit-conversion reminder before a new answer.

fields.question: How do static and dynamic critique selection differ?
fields.answer: Static uses frequent global failures; dynamic retrieves relevant CritBank entries for the current input. Both act before generation, but only dynamic adds input-dependent retrieval.
fields.example: A math question can retrieve calculation reminders different from those for other requests.

fields.question: Why not select critiques with the current question's correct answer?
fields.answer: That leaks evaluation targets into prompts. Dynamic retrieval uses only input similarity to the existing bank and then generates once. Offline failures and current hidden gold stay separate.
fields.example: Looking up the solution before picking the critique that fixes it is not deployable retrieval.

fields.question: Why not replace cross-lingual semantic aggregation with string voting, and why count aggregation cost?
fields.answer: Different languages may phrase equivalent facts differently, and superficially similar errors can differ. The method uses an LM for majority/minority-aware aggregation and separate correctness/consistency judgment. All path and aggregation tokens count. This is literature-only locally.
fields.example: Two names for one city need entity matching, not separate votes or costs counted from only one path.

fields.question: Why explore multiple languages for one knowledge question?
fields.answer: Knowledge may be more accessible under some language contexts. Explore across languages then aggregate semantic answers, not mere string translations or presumed-correct majority.
fields.example: Distinct expressions may refer to one entity.

fields.question: Why can't a string counter substitute for semantic model aggregation?
fields.answer: Equivalent meanings can use different strings and equal strings can differ in context. An LM performs majority/minority-aware aggregation and semantic judgments in the paper.
fields.example: “United States” and “USA” can be one answer, despite string counts splitting them.

fields.question: Why count more than generated path tokens?
fields.answer: Include each path's inputs and aggregation model tokens; semantic correctness and consistency also use model calls. Local work did not run the APIs or provide heuristics as substitutes.
fields.example: Ten short generations can still produce a long, expensive aggregation prompt.

fields.question: Why fix prediction order and isolate gold in grouped DeepSEA reporting?
fields.answer: Validate language, size, and order so predictions align to their examples. Expose only public task fields; keep answers and annotations with the evaluator. This evaluates lower-resource languages, not model training.
fields.example: Swapped outputs across languages become alignment errors; the predictor must not see references.

fields.question: Why not report only one DeepSEA multilingual average?
fields.answer: Language-resource strata and tasks expose gaps hidden by a mean. The project provides data and evaluation protocol, not a parameter-training algorithm.
fields.example: High-resource successes can mask low-resource failures.

fields.question: Are deterministic scorers and LLM judges interchangeable in DeepSEA?
fields.answer: Follow the fixed upstream protocol for each task. Substituting judges changes comparability. Bind outputs to language, subject, and row; group summaries do not fix misalignment.
fields.example: Pairing language A row one with a language B answer invalidates scoring even if row counts match.

fields.question: Should prediction callbacks get the evaluator or benchmark file and promise not to read gold?
fields.answer: No. Use allowlisted immutable public input and separate deep-copied private references. Reject missing languages, bad counts, or nonstring outputs. This is data-flow isolation, not an OS sandbox; do not add shell bypasses.
fields.example: Provide question, options, and context, not raw answer_with_cot records.

fields.question: Why is zeroing a DetectorScope concept exact in logit space but not equivalent to editing text?
fields.answer: Sparse pooled features feed a linear head, so each weight times activation is an exact contribution. Text edits can change several features and contexts. Automatic descriptions are imperfect; local head excludes the full SAE/explanation pipeline.
fields.example: Zero one feature to verify its score change; deleting a word can alter several concepts.

fields.question: Why make detection depend on inspectable sparse features?
fields.answer: Pool SAE features, filter unreliable concept descriptions, and fit a sparse linear head so logits decompose into actual computed contributions rather than post-hoc reasons.
fields.example: Verify a contribution by zeroing its feature rather than trusting generated explanations.

fields.question: Is description validation equivalent to human confirmation of concept semantics?
fields.answer: Spearman correlation compares observed and predicted activation ranks as a filter, not manual validation or safety. Constant sequences do not support the correlation.
fields.example: Correlation on a small sample does not prove meanings are correct for every text.

fields.question: Why not apply an L1 subgradient and soft thresholding together?
fields.answer: Apply BCE SGD with momentum, then ηλ soft thresholding, without a second L1 gradient or bias penalty. Fit uncentered RMS on training only.
fields.example: Penalizing twice changes effective sparsity beyond λ.

fields.question: Why doesn't label-free FUSE get more reliable simply by adding correlated verifiers?
fields.answer: Moment estimation needs identifiability assumptions such as a better-than-random majority and conditionally independent triplets. Transforms mitigate correlation, but shared errors can remain. Posteriors are not gold, which stays evaluation-only.
fields.example: Three verifiers copying one wrong rule are not three independent correctness signals.

fields.question: Why not average verifier scores in FUSE?
fields.answer: Correlated errors get counted repeatedly. Estimate query-conditioned quality from scores, transform to mitigate dependencies, then build posteriors for ensemble optimization.
fields.example: Three near-identical verifiers need not add three times the evidence.

fields.question: Do moment-based posteriors provide the same guarantees as gold labels?
fields.answer: No. They depend on identifiability; high correlation or constant scores can break estimation. High estimated probability is not truth or safety.
fields.example: Shared wrong rules can produce agreement on the wrong answer.

fields.question: Can gold choose score transforms or ensemble parameters?
fields.answer: Not in the documented label-free fit. Use score matrices only and reserve labels for independent evaluation. Choosing transforms by gold on the same questions breaks both boundaries.
fields.example: Trying transforms and selecting the best by answers is not unsupervised selection.

fields.question: Why swap both word identity and document order in conflict tests?
fields.answer: Order alone confounds lexical preference, source role, and position. Four orthogonal crossings estimate effects, with a shared filtered set and unfiltered sensitivity analysis. Conclusions are for one model on short English choices.
fields.example: A favored word can win in either position; swap which source provides it to isolate source and order.

fields.question: Why use a multiway crossing for two-document conflicts?
fields.answer: Word identity, source, and position can all influence choice. Four conditions separate them instead of mistaking lexical or ordering preference for trust.
fields.example: Preferring word B is different from preferring whichever word the new source supplies.

fields.question: Why distinguish order null contrast O from positional effect S?
fields.answer: They use different sign combinations. S measures position and negative S favors first; O is a null control. Both are half effects, so double for full range.
fields.example: Changing the signs on e1–e4 yields a different contrast.

fields.question: Can failed or degenerate BCa intervals silently fall back to equivalence?
fields.answer: No. Keep failed/degenerate and equivalent=null, not a hidden percentile interval. Ten conditions share the union of exclusions, and unfiltered sensitivity remains.
fields.example: If bootstrap cannot form a valid interval, report undecided rather than a pass.

fields.question: Why is λ=0 still calibrated in interpolated null calibration?
fields.answer: Zero removes the instruction-null contribution but still subtracts bare-null. Align all three score vectors by document and select λ on validation. A global oracle weight is not held-out gain. Local work is a score kernel.
fields.example: A long document can score highly without a query; bare-null still removes this baseline.

fields.question: Why compare instruction null with bare null in attention reranking?
fields.answer: Instructions can affect scores even without a query. Interpolation separates that influence and controls which baseline is subtracted from query-plus-instruction scores.
fields.example: “Judge relevance” may raise document scores without conveying the user's query.
